THE FINDING THAT MATTERED: a DSSE signature covers the envelope's Pre-Authentication Encoding ('DSSEv1' SP LEN(type) SP type SP LEN(body) SP body), NOT the payload bytes — established by checking real cosign output byte-for-byte before writing verifier code. Signing the payload directly would verify something an attacker can re-wrap. ORGANIZING CLAIM, and the reason the document is short rather than a daemon-spec clone: a leaf is not a smaller daemon. It is the same ABI with the service graph decided at BUILD time instead of at boot, and every other difference — no management API, no filesystem, no hot-install, no registry — follows from that rather than being separately chosen. §1 states it as a table.

THE ENGINE SECTION IS MEASURED, WHICH IS WHY THIS COULD NOT HAVE BEEN WRITTEN BEFORE eieio-x7g.3. Cited from crates/conformance/tests/wamr.rs: 31 of 32 scenarios pass; WAMR refuses all nine proposals outside the accepted six INCLUDING the three wasm3 runs, so a WAMR leaf needs no carve-out of its own; WAMR runs the whole of bulk memory and reference types where wasm3 runs part, which widens nothing because §4.3's subset is the floor across leaf engines; and WAMR's rejections name no proposal, being opcode- and section-level parse errors.

BUDGETS ARE A WATCHDOG, NOT FUEL, and that is a finding rather than a preference: wasm_runtime_set_instruction_count_limit exists in WAMR's C API but is compiled out behind WASM_ENABLE_INSTRUCTION_METERING, established by a linker error rather than by reading documentation. wasm3 has no counter at all. This is exactly why the conformance harness lets a host answer enforces_budgets = false and skip 07_budget_exhausted by name — a binding without a watchdog is honest instead of hanging.

THE FOUR OBLIGATIONS THE 2026-08-09 EPIC REVIEW REQUIRED, all present as normative sections:
1. §3.1 — the engine as the only feature-set enforcement point, stated CONCRETELY per engine (WAMR selects features at CMake build time, not through a runtime config object; wasm3 has no switches and its acceptance was measured instruction by instruction). Plus: neither engine can express the carve-out, so a leaf MUST run eio_manifest::validate, at firmware build time where a refusal costs a build rather than a field failure.
2. §9.1 — ABI 6.3.1's two RFC 8949 deviations, with the warning stated as a heading: a stock canonical-CBOR encoder is WRONG for this platform. Binary64-always, and map keys sorted by UTF-8 content rather than encoded bytes.
3. §4.1 — decode depth bound MUST be at least the configured MAX_DEPTH, with why: a lower bound makes a value the language is required to handle undecodable, turning an EXPR 9 budget into a decode failure with a different error code on one host only.
4. §9 — the leaf runs the ABI 13 suite, expr-tests and the CBOR vectors AT ITS OWN BUDGET SETTINGS, not the reference defaults, because a floor that holds only on a generous host is not a floor.

WHAT I DID NOT DECIDE. §6.1's AOT pipeline is PROPOSED and explicitly unratified: wamrc has never been built on any machine here (eieio-7d8.21's six blockers), so the artifact layout comes from WAMR's documentation rather than from anything this repository has produced, and it ratifies when a leaf loads an artifact the pipeline built. The WAMR/LLVM 18 pairing IS normative, because a mismatch is a load failure in the field after flashing. The MQTT client is deliberately unnamed — rumqttc is std, a leaf needs no_std or embedded-nal, and nothing has been measured. Flash wear budget policy went to SCOPE 3.7 as a new OPEN rather than being guessed at, per this bead's own acceptance criterion.

THE DECISION AND ITS REASONING, recorded because this will be re-litigated. An optional advisory declaration in ABI 11.1 — a block MAY name the attributes a port emits or expects — was the alternative and was declined on three grounds: every declaration is a thing that can be wrong; a block whose output shape depends on its input cannot state one honestly; and the failure it would prevent is already caught loudly at the first signal, because EXPR 6 makes a missing attribute a per-signal error rather than a null. Signals being dict-shaped and dynamic is a deliberate choice this platform has made repeatedly, not an omission waiting to be filled.

The third option — derive fields by watching a tap and remembering what was seen — was also on the table and was not chosen as the mechanism, but DESIGNER 5 now names observed tap traffic as one legitimate SOURCE for the hint, alongside a block's documentation and what its properties reference. That keeps the option open without making design-time help depend on having already run the service.

WHAT THE SPEC NOW REQUIRES, and this is the part that matters for correctness: the hint is best-effort, and it may be ABSENT — which is the ordinary case for a block nobody has run. Absent means UNKNOWN, never "this port carries nothing". A modal that rendered an empty hint as a fact would be asserting something no one declared, so it renders nothing instead. The hint's job is to save an operator from guessing, not to become a schema the platform does not have.

The TypeScript field carries the same note in place, where someone would otherwise reasonably mistake PortDescriptor.fields for a manifest field — which is exactly what the m9s.2 agent flagged when it added the extension and labelled it non-ABI rather than passing it off as standard. ABI 7.0's six host functions now exist ONCE, in host-core, per DAEMON 1.1 (written for this bead before any code). Argument decoding, ABI 8's status and size convention, the emission ledger and rand's bounds proof are shared.

The entropy split is why it had to stay injectable rather than being folded in: the daemon takes the OS's, the leaf a bring-up PRNG, and the conformance harness a DETERMINISTIC one, because ABI 13.1 needs a suite to get the same bytes twice.

THE FINDING IS WORTH MORE THAN THE REFACTOR, and it is the reason to insist a negative proof actually bites. What rand's pre-check is the ONLY thing standing in front of is a PARTIAL WRITE: a small, genuinely in-bounds buf with a len chosen so buf + len wraps 32 bits back into something that also looks in-bounds. Then the first 4096-byte chunk draws its bytes and lands in guest memory before the second correctly fails.

That case now has its own test (rand_refuses_an_overflowing_range_before_writing_a_single_chunk, buf=4096, len=4_294_963_401, 8192-byte memory) and the module doc records why the naive out-of-bounds case proves nothing. Anyone who hits a mystifying cold-build wall on macOS can find this bead by searching for the symptom.

daemon-v0.1.0 published. Release run 33776508539: ci, both build jobs (x86_64 and aarch64), smoke and publish all green — publish being the one step that had never run and could not be rehearsed, since gh release create needs a real tag.

The release carries exactly the four artifacts the acceptance asked for, verified by reading them off the release rather than off the workflow: eio-daemon-{x86_64,aarch64}-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz and both .sha256. The completeness guard — the loop asserting both files exist for both targets before gh release create runs — was therefore observed passing on a real run.

THE FIRST ATTEMPT AT THIS TAG FAILED, and not because of anything in the daemon: it stopped at the ci gate, which had been red since 2026-08-24 for two reasons. designer/dist was gitignored, so rust-embed could not compile crates/designer on a fresh checkout; and the runner had no wasm-pack, so test-designer failed rather than degrading. A third fix followed — the parity suites shelled out to cargo from inside vitest while the test stage held the target-dir lock, timing out the hook on a cold runner. All three landed before this tag was re-cut onto a green commit.

Worth recording because it is the more useful finding than the release itself: for ten days a local 'just ci' passed while CI failed, and every gate-green report in that window was the wrong gate.

Every child is closed and the epic's own subject is now proven end to end rather than rehearsed.

The last two were eieio-p0k.8 (cut the first daemon-v* tag) and eieio-p0k.9 (the macOS first-exec scanning measurement, closed as an environment problem rather than a repository one). daemon-v0.1.0 is published with all four artifacts and the completeness guard observed passing on a real run.

WHAT THIS EPIC ENDED UP BEING WORTH, beyond the pipelines themselves: the release attempt is what surfaced that CI had been red since 2026-08-24 while a local 'just ci' passed. Three separate causes, none of them the daemon's — a gitignored designer/dist that rust-embed cannot compile without, a runner with no wasm-pack, and the parity suites shelling out to cargo from inside vitest while the test stage held the target-directory lock. All three are fixed and CI is green.

Reopen if the release-sdk or release-designer pipelines need the same first-real-tag treatment; neither has been exercised against a real tag either, and they are separate workflows on separate tag prefixes (sdk-v*, designer-v*). Worth a bead each when someone means to publish them — release-sdk is the one that touches crates.io.
